topic: Where your lunch goes, and how big your gut really is inside

sources.title: Human Gut Has The Surface Area Of A Studio Apartment
Your Digestive System & How It Works
sources.publisher: U.S. National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)

claims.text: Textbooks said the gut's inner surface was about 300 m², a tennis court; a 2014 study measured about 32 m², half a badminton court.
claims.quote: say the surface area of the human gut is about 300 square meters, or about the size of a tennis court; is not in the order of tennis lawn,” they wrote, “but rather is that of half a badminton court

claims.text: The small intestine's inner surface averages about 30 m²; the whole gut about 32 m².
claims.quote: averages 30 square metres; found the average surface area of the human gut is actually about 32 square meters

claims.text: A ring-like muscle lets food into the stomach.
claims.quote: a ringlike muscle—called the lower esophageal sphincter —relaxes and lets food pass into your stomach

claims.text: After four or five hours the stomach has emptied.
claims.quote: After four or five hours the stomach has emptied

claims.text: The liver makes about 400-800 ml of bile a day, which helps emulsify fat.
claims.quote: About 400 to 800 milliliters; helping to emulsify the lipids in food

claims.text: The liver's functions are generally cited as around 500.
claims.quote: Estimates regarding the organ's total number of functions vary, but are generally cited as being around 500
claims.label: estimates vary

claims.text: Folds, villi and microvilli enlarge the small intestine's surface for absorption.
claims.quote: due to enlargement caused by folds, villi and microvilli
Your large intestine absorbs water, and the waste products of digestion become stool

claims.text: Bacteria in the large intestine break down food.
claims.quote: Bacteria in the large intestine can also break down food

myths.myth: Your gut's inner surface is the size of a tennis court.
myths.truth: About 30-32 m², half a badminton court (Helander & Fändriks 2014).
